source.title_on_document: Long-term impact of ChatGPT-4 on music students' creative and analytical skills: A follow-up study

supplement.where: The document refers to no supplementary material, online appendix, or supporting information, and the end matter on p. 17 has no such section. Data availability: 'Data for this study is available on request from the corresponding author.' (p. 17)
supplement.holds: Nothing. No participant-level standard deviations by arm are printed anywhere. The main text gives growth-model estimates with standard errors (Table 3), MANCOVA and univariate F tests (Tables 4-5), and adjusted means with standard errors (Table 6).

paper_design_summary: The paper reports class-level random assignment to ChatGPT-4-supported or traditional teacher-led music coursework and analyzes 74 second-year Bachelor of Music students in South Korea (36 experimental, 38 control; p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 12, Table 6), although it labels the design quasi-experimental. During the 24-week intervention, students submitted creative products and analytical tasks every two weeks, and two blinded external experts scored them on seven-point rubrics at 12 measurement points (pp. 5-8, Sections 3.2-3.6). The paper compares creativity using latent growth models and MANCOVA adjusted for prior ChatGPT use and Week 1 scores, and separately examines relationships with analytical skills and the experimental group's interaction logs (pp. 8-12).

studies.label: 24-week classroom intervention: ChatGPT-4-supported vs traditional music instruction

assignment.what_was_assigned: Instructional condition for ordinary two-semester music coursework: ChatGPT-4 integrated into learning tasks versus traditional teacher-led instruction without AI, both taught by the same instructor. Section 3.1 explicitly says participants were randomly assigned and specifies that the random assignment was at the class level. The number of classes and allocation procedure are not stated; the abstract and Section 3.1 also call the design quasi-experimental. randomized = yes records the explicit reported allocation, and does not mean that students were independently randomized within classes.
assignment.quote: While the random assignment was conducted at the class level (an unavoidable constraint of the institutional timetable), the design still ensured balance in demographic characteristics and musical background across groups.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1, third paragraph (explicit random assignment and class-level unit); p. 5, first paragraph and p. 1, Abstract (quasi-experimental label; the abstract itself does not claim random assignment)

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT-4 supported)
arms.description: Integrated ChatGPT-4 into the weekly learning cycle as a scaffold for creative exploration and analytical reasoning in composition, improvisation, harmonic analysis, transcription, and arranging: generating alternative melodic or harmonic suggestions, drafting programme notes, and receiving simulated feedback on compositional decisions. Students were encouraged to critically evaluate, adapt, and integrate the output, and they shared screenshots or links of their ChatGPT interactions (pp. 5-7, Table 1).

arms.name: Control (traditional instruction)
arms.description: Completed equivalent tasks with textbooks, class notes, lectures, handouts, and teacher consultation. Feedback came from the instructor without AI mediation. Same instructor as the experimental group (pp. 5-6, Table 1).

participants.exclusions: No post-assignment exclusions or withdrawals are reported. Of 86 students in the music programme, 12 took part only in the pilot and not in the main study (p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 7, Section 3.4). Table 6 lists 36 experimental and 38 control students analyzed (p. 12). Levene's tests use F(1, 72) (p. 9), and the univariate tests use df2 = 69 (p. 12, Table 5), consistent with 74 people analyzed.
participants.who: Second-year undergraduates in the Bachelor of Music programme, drawn from the cohort of the authors' earlier short-term ChatGPT-4 study (Zhou & Kim, 2024).
participants.quote: Participants were seventy-four second-year undergraduates enrolled in the Bachelor of Music programme at a university in South Korea.
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1; group sizes p. 5, p. 1 Abstract, and p. 12, Table 6

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (the paper also calls it 'the newer generation of ChatGPT-4 (i.e., ChatGPT-4o)', p. 5)
ai_tool.how_used: Used throughout the weekly tasks through guided prompts: suggesting melodic, harmonic, and structural ideas, revising with AI feedback, generating improvisation tasks and stylistic models, suggesting corrections and reharmonizations, checking rhythmic accuracy and harmonic labeling, suggesting voicing and orchestration, and giving simulated feedback. Students were encouraged to critically evaluate, adapt, and integrate the output into their own work, and they submitted screenshots or links of their ChatGPT interactions (p. 5; p. 6, Table 1; p. 7, Section 3.6). The use mixes supplied ideas and refinement within free chatbot use.

task.description: Music coursework in five sequential themes: composition (melody writing, motif development, thematic variation, small ensemble writing), improvisation, harmonic analysis (including reharmonization), stylistic transcription, and applied arranging. Every two weeks students submitted a creative product (e.g., a composition or improvisation) and an analytical task (e.g., harmonic labeling or structural justification).
task.duration: 24 weeks over two semesters (October 2024 to January 2025 and March to June 2025); 12 measurement points (pp. 5, 7-8).

outcomes.name: Creativity rubric score (expert-rated) of submitted creative products
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric adapted from Webster's (2002) model of creative thinking in music and Burnard's (2012) application of the Consensual Assessment Technique. Four dimensions, each on a seven-point scale: originality of musical ideas, overall musical value, inventiveness in development, and expressive impact (pp. 6-7, Section 3.3). The paper does not state how the four dimensions or the two raters' scores combine into one score, and reports no inter-rater reliability for the output-scoring rubrics (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5). The interaction-log coding reliability in Section 3.3 is a separate measure. Two external assessors with expertise in music theory, composition, and creativity research scored all submissions, blinded to identity, group, and timing. Discrepancies over two points on a dimension were resolved by discussion (p. 7, Section 3.5). Analyzed two ways: (a) a linear latent growth model over the 12 measurement points, estimated per group (Table 3, Fig. 1); (b) a MANCOVA with follow-up univariate tests, with prior ChatGPT use, Week 1 creativity, and Week 1 analytical scores as covariates (Tables 4-6). The paper does not state which time point or aggregate the MANCOVA dependent variable uses.

contrasts.reported: Follow-up univariate test after the MANCOVA (covariates: prior ChatGPT use, Week 1 creativity, Week 1 analytical), Group on Creativity: df1 = 1, df2 = 69, F = 7.216, p = .009, η² = .096 (Table 5). Adjusted means: Experimental 4.71 (Std. Error 0.18, N = 36) vs Control 4.35 (Std. Error 0.17, N = 38) (Table 6). Multivariate Group effect on creativity and analytical skills together: Pillai's Trace = .047, df1 = 2, df2 = 68, F = 3.982, p = .023, η² = .047 (Table 4). The paper prints η² without saying whether it is partial.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Results RQ2; p. 11, Table 4; p. 12, Tables 5 and 6

contrasts.reported: Linear latent growth model of creativity, estimated per group (Table 3): Experimental intercept 3.281 (Std. Err. 0.043, p < .000), slope 0.315 (Std. Err. 0.006, p < .000); Control intercept 3.004 (Std. Err. 0.064, p < .000), slope 0.210 (Std. Err. 0.010, p < .000). Text: 'The slope estimate for creativity was 0.32 in the experimental group, compared with 0.21 in the control group' (p. 8). No test of the group difference in intercept or slope is printed. Fig. 1 plots estimated mean scores by group from wk1 to wk12 (p. 10). Linear model fit for creativity: CFI = .961, TLI = .953, RMSEA = .021, SRMR = .032 (Table 2, p. 6).
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Results RQ1; p. 9, Table 3; p. 10, Fig. 1; p. 6, Table 2

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Zhou, W., & Kim, Y. (2024). Innovative music education: An empirical assessment of ChatGPT-4's impact on student learning experiences. Education and Information Technologies, 29, 20855-20881. Same cohort. The introduction describes that study as having '74 undergraduate music students in Korea' (p. 2). The present paper collects new data in a new 24-week intervention and does not reanalyze the earlier data. In the earlier study only the AI-condition students received structured ChatGPT-supported learning, so prior ChatGPT use is a covariate here. Whether students kept their earlier condition is not stated.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met on the reported allocation: participants 'were randomly assigned to one of two groups', and 'the random assignment was conducted at the class level' (p. 5, Section 3.1). The intervention supplies generative-AI assistance for students' own creative coursework, with an otherwise equivalent no-AI comparison (pp. 5-7, Sections 3.1-3.2, Table 1, and Section 3.6). The quasi-experimental label and missing allocation details are reporting limitations, but the paper explicitly reports random class assignment and describes no contrary non-random allocation procedure. The codebook and form spec set no minimum number of classes per arm; they define quasi_people by non-random assignment. Thus an unstated class count does not by itself negate criterion 1, and even one class per arm would not establish non-random allocation. Class counts and uncertainty that reflects class-level assignment remain necessary for evaluating precision and pooling (codebook Section 10). Criterion 2 is met: 74 people were analyzed, with 36 and 38 in Table 6 (p. 12), consistent with the assignment counts in Section 3.1 (p. 5); pilot-only students are outside this sample. Criterion 3 is met: two blinded external experts scored submitted musical products on a four-dimension, seven-point creativity rubric (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5). The outcome answers with_ai because the experimental group had ChatGPT-4 available during the scored coursework (p. 6, Table 1; p. 7, Section 3.6); AI withdrawal is proposed as future research (p. 16, Section 5.3).

one_line_finding: Among 74 music students analyzed in a study reporting class-level random assignment, the ChatGPT-4 group had higher adjusted expert-rated creativity than the traditional-instruction group (4.71 vs 4.35; F(1, 69) = 7.216, p = .009, η² = .096; p. 12, Tables 5-6) and a steeper reported creativity growth slope (0.315 vs 0.210; p. 9, Table 3).
open_questions: How many classes were assigned to each arm, how was the reported class randomization implemented, and how should class-level assignment be reflected in the uncertainty estimates? Section 3.1 reports random class assignment but gives no class count or procedure (p. 5), and Sections 3.7 and 4 describe no class-clustered analysis (pp. 8-9; Tables 5-6, p. 12). The codebook sets no minimum number of classes for eligibility.

Which time point or aggregate defines the MANCOVA dependent variable? The text does not say (p. 9, Results RQ2). Table 6 gives adjusted means, while Fig. 1 depicts the latent growth trajectory; approximate graph endpoints are not treated as printed statistics (pp. 10, 12).

Were the Week 1 scores produced before the intervention began? The paper calls them baseline scores (p. 9) and says baseline tasks preceded the intervention (p. 5), but Table 1 places ChatGPT-supported composition in Weeks 1-5 (p. 6).

Where are the baseline comparability tests? The balance claim cites Tables 1 and 2 (p. 5), but Table 1 describes instruction and Table 2 reports growth-model fit (p. 6). The abstract says the experimental group began with higher initial levels, and Table 3 reports different creativity intercepts (pp. 1, 9).

How do calendar weeks map to measurement occasions? The paper reports 12 biweekly time points over 24 weeks (pp. 5, 7-8), but also speaks of weekly assessments (p. 5), an entire semester (p. 2), and weeks 1 to 12 in Fig. 1 and the cross-lagged and ENA analyses (pp. 9-10).

Did students retain the condition they had in Zhou and Kim (2024), and how did earlier condition relate to the present class allocation? This is not stated; the present paper reports current random class assignment and adjusts for prior ChatGPT use (p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 8, Section 3.7).

Can the authors provide participant-level standard deviations by arm and analysis data with class identifiers? No participant-level arm SDs are printed; Table 6 gives adjusted means and standard errors (p. 12). The paper offers data on request and identifies no supplement or posted dataset (p. 17).

How were the creativity rubric dimensions and the two assessors' ratings combined, and what is the inter-rater reliability of the output scores? Sections 3.3 and 3.5 do not specify this (pp. 6-7); the reported interaction-log coding reliability concerns a different assessment.

Which multivariate test values should be used after checking the original analysis output? Table 4 reports Group Pillai's Trace = .047 alongside F(2, 68) = 3.982 (p. 11), which are inconsistent under the standard single-effect Pillai conversion. The printed values are retained pending author clarification.
notes: The search record guessed after_ai from the 'long-term' title. All rated products were made during the intervention, with ChatGPT-4 available to the treatment group, so the outcome answers with_ai. The paper names AI withdrawal as future work: 'Future research must therefore ask whether these patterns persist once the AI is withdrawn' (p. 16). Not listed as outcomes: (1) The analytical-thinking rubric (p. 7), which is not a creativity construct. Its statistics match the PDF: Table 3 intercepts 2.973 (Std. Err. 0.038) vs 2.621 (0.056), slopes 0.336 (0.005) vs 0.282 (0.009); Table 5 Group F(1, 69) = 5.482, p = .022, η² = .075; Table 6 adjusted means 4.67 (SE 0.16, N = 36) vs 4.38 (SE 0.16, N = 38); Fig. 2, p. 11. (2) The cross-lagged panel model (Table 7, p. 12): Analytic(t-1) to Creativity(t) β = 0.34-0.70 (experimental) vs 0.18-0.40 (control), Wald χ² = 21.47, p < .001; creativity autoregression 0.20-0.28 vs 0.32-0.57, Wald χ² = 19.16, p < .001; end-point correlation r = 0.74 vs r = 0.19 (ns). (3) Epistemic network analysis and first-order Markov transitions of coded ChatGPT interaction logs, which cover the experimental group only (N = 36, Table 8, p. 14; Figs. 3-6, pp. 13-16) and have no AI vs no-AI contrast. Creativity growth-model random effects are in the text (pp. 8-9): intercept-slope covariance Est. = 0.004, p = .012 (experimental) and Est. = -0.003, p = .028 (control). The pilot used 12 students from the same programme outside the sample (pp. 5, 7). The authors used ChatGPT to improve the manuscript's language (p. 17). Reconciliation note: form B's assignment quote read 'the unavoidable constraint'. The PDF reads 'an unavoidable constraint' (p. 5), and this form uses the PDF wording. Finalization: the full markdown, including all references and end matter, was read; the PDF contains no appendix or identified supplement. All retained reported statistics were checked against the PDF text/tables, and Fig. 1 was inspected. Approximate graph endpoint values were removed from open_questions rather than retained as reported statistics. The Table 3 p-values are preserved as printed (< .000), without silently correcting them. The Table 4 Group trace/F inconsistency remains an author query; no substitute estimate has been computed. The explicit class-level randomization report determines design_class = field_rct and criterion 1 = met; the quasi-experimental label, unknown class counts, and missing class-level uncertainty are retained as reporting and precision limitations. No minimum class count appears in the supplied eligibility rules. Class-level assignment must be reflected in uncertainty before an estimate is pooled; 74 analyzed people does not imply 74 independent randomized units. This is new follow-up data from the earlier cohort, not a reanalysis of the earlier experiment. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as requested; final and eligibility supersede its earlier unclear-core decision and its claim that one class per arm necessarily implies non-random assignment. The reconciliation contains no unresolved differences. Challenge counts count problems in the challenge files, not the separate extraction questions in final.open_items.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1 design_class = field_rct and assignment.randomized = yes were challenged because the paper uses a quasi-experimental label, gives no class count or allocation procedure, and may have one class per arm.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Retained field_rct, randomized = yes, unit = class, and the reported assignment counts. The PDF explicitly reports random assignment at the class level; the abstract's quasi-experimental label does not document a non-random allocation mechanism. The form spec defines quasi_people by non-random assignment, and neither it nor the codebook requires several classes per arm. One class per arm would limit independent replication and inference, but would not by itself make a reported random allocation non-random. Changed eligibility.core to yes, criterion 1 to met, and context_class to none; clarified that the randomization claim comes from Section 3.1, not the abstract. Missing class counts, implementation details, and class-adjusted uncertainty remain author queries. The reconciliation object is unchanged.
challenge_resolution.quote: While the random assignment was conducted at the class level (an unavoidable constraint of the institutional timetable), the design still ensured balance in demographic characteristics and musical background across groups.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Class counts, allocation implementation, and class-adjusted uncertainty are unreported (pp. 5, 8-9, 12).
